views.name: city_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  city.city_name AS city_name,
  city.population AS population,
  city.state_name AS state_name,
  city.country_name AS country_name
FROM city

params.description: Provides one-row-per-city core attributes (city name, population, state_name, country_name) for answering city-level population and membership queries.
params.when_to_use: Ask which cities within a specific state (e.g., Wyoming, Texas) have the largest population or meet a population threshold — the view is one-row-per-city so filtering by state_name and ordering or comparing population works (validated by questions about largest city in Wyoming, cities in Wyoming above-average population, and cities in Texas relative to the state max). | Compare city populations within a state (e.g., find cities with population > X% of the state's maximum) by querying city_core.population grouped/filtered by city_core.state_name. | List city attributes (name, population, state, country) for lookups and UI dropdowns when one-row-per-city is desired.
params.output_schema: city_name: city.city_name (city name string from table city) | population: city.population (population numeric from table city) | state_name: city.state_name (state name string from table city) | country_name: city.country_name (country name string from table city)
params.metric: population = city.population (city-level population as stored in city table)
params.composition: Cardinality-safe: join city_core (one-row-per-city) to a one-row-per-state table ON city_core.state_name = state.state_name only if the state-side is indeed one row per state — this will not duplicate city population. | Cardinality-safe: join city_core to a one-row-per-country table ON city_core.country_name = country.country_name only if the country-side is one row per country. | Do NOT join city_core directly to tables that have multiple rows per city (one-to-many children) without aggregating the child table first (e.g., GROUP BY city_name) because such joins will multiply city rows and cause population to be duplicated. | When aggregating up (e.g., compute state population), explicitly aggregate city_core.population by state_name (e.g., SELECT state_name, SUM(population) FROM city_core GROUP BY state_name). | When joining by name keys, ensure exact match / canonicalization of state_name and country_name between sources, because the view exposes only textual keys.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need a different grain than one-row-per-city (for example, neighborhood- or person-level analysis) because this view exposes only city-level rows and will undercount or be incompatible with more granular measures. | Avoid using this view to join directly to child tables that are one-to-many with respect to city (e.g., events, neighborhoods, residents) without first aggregating the many-side, because joining will multiply city rows and duplicate city-level population values. | Do not rely on state_name or country_name as stable foreign keys if the other table uses canonical IDs; the view only exposes textual name columns — joins by name can be incorrect if names are not standardized or unique.
params.dialect_notes: SQLite SQL (the view selects directly from table 'city' without schema qualifiers).

views.name: state_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.state_name AS state_name,
  s.population AS population,
  s.area AS area,
  s.country_name AS country_name,
  s.capital AS capital,
  s.density AS density
FROM state s

params.description: Provides one-row-per-state attributes (state_name, population, area, country_name, capital, density) useful for answering questions about state-level properties and comparisons (e.g., which state has highest density) and for attaching state attributes when asking about a specific state's cities.
params.when_to_use: Answer state-level comparison questions that rely on state attributes present here (e.g., which state has highest density, which state's inhabitants appear most densely packed) because the view is one row per state with precomputed density. | Attach state attributes when the question focuses on a specific state and you need state metadata (e.g., identifying cities in Wyoming or asking which city in Wyoming is largest) — use state_core to filter or provide the state's attributes while querying city-level tables. | Compute aggregates where the grain is states (e.g., SUM(state_core.population) GROUP BY state_core.country_name) because state_core is one-row-per-state and contains population and area for each state.
params.output_schema: state_name: state name (from state.state_name) | population: state population (from state.population) | area: state area (from state.area) | country_name: country name that the state belongs to (from state.country_name) | capital: state's capital name (from state.capital) | density: precomputed population density for the state (from state.density)
params.grounded_columns: state.state_name | state.population | state.area | state.country_name | state.capital | state.density
params.metric: density = state.density  -- precomputed density column selected unchanged from state table
params.composition: Cardinality-safe: join to one-row-per-country tables on country_name (state_core.country_name = country.country_name) because state_core is one-row-per-state. | When joining to city-level or other many-rows-per-state tables, first aggregate the many-side to one row per state (e.g., COUNT(*) AS city_count_by_state GROUP BY city_state_name) and then join that aggregated result to state_core on state_name to avoid duplicating state-level measures. | To compute higher-grain aggregates (e.g., country population), aggregate state_core (SUM(population) GROUP BY country_name) rather than relying on joins that could multiply state rows.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse when you need city-level or other many-per-state facts as source of detail (e.g., listing all cities or counting cities) because state_core has one row per state and does not contain city rows or city-level counts. | Avoid using state_core as a direct substitute for pre-aggregated results of many-to-one joins: joining state_core to a table that has many rows per state without first aggregating the many-side will duplicate or distort state measures (wrong join/grain), because state_core is one-row-per-state and the SQL has no joins or aggregations to reconcile many-sided data. | Do not use this view when the desired answer depends on a different cohort or grouping than state_name (for example, if you need sub-state geographies or country-level rows only) because the view's grain is explicitly state_name and it selects directly from state s without grouping or filtering.
params.dialect_notes: Dialect: SQLite. The view selects directly from table alias 'state s' and makes no use of dialect-specific functions; no special SQL syntax required.

views.name: cities_by_state_ranked
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.city_name,
  c.state_name,
  c.population,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c.state_name ORDER BY c.population DESC) AS city_rank_within_state
FROM city_core c

params.description: List of cities with their state, population, and the city's rank by population within its state.
params.when_to_use: Find the population rank of a specific city within its state (e.g., 'what is Boston's rank within Massachusetts?'). | Compare cities within the same state by population (e.g., 'show top N cities by population in each state'). | Compose higher-level aggregations that need city-level population and position within state (e.g., select all cities with rank <= 3 per state). | Drive reports or filters that need one row per city with its intra-state rank available for downstream logic.
params.output_schema: city_name: The city's name. Derived directly from base table column city_core.city_name. | state_name: The state's name that the city belongs to. Derived directly from base table column city_core.state_name. | population: The city's population. Derived directly from base table column city_core.population. | city_rank_within_state: The population rank of the city within its state (1 = highest population). Derived from the window expression RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city_core.state_name ORDER BY city_core.population DESC).
params.metric: city_rank_within_state = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city_core.state_name ORDER BY city_core.population DESC) | population = city_core.population (base metric/column, not aggregated in this view)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_core on state_core.state_name = cities_by_state_ranked.state_name — safe because cities_by_state_ranked is one row per city (grain = city_name) and joining to a one-row-per-state table will not duplicate city rows; state-level attributes can be appended without changing city-level measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to city_core on city_core.city_name = cities_by_state_ranked.city_name AND city_core.state_name = cities_by_state_ranked.state_name — safe as a PK re-attach to the originating base row (reproduces same city row), but unnecessary because the view already exposes those base columns. | unsafe-to-join guidance: do NOT join this view directly to any table or view that is one-to-many relative to the city grain (for example: city_events, city_neighborhoods, transactions_by_city) without first aggregating the many-side to one row per city. Doing so will multiply city rows and therefore duplicate the population and rank measures. | unsafe-to-join guidance: do NOT join to other city-level ranking or aggregated views that are not at the same exact city_name grain and same de-duplication semantics unless you align on (city_name, state_name); mismatched grain joins can produce incorrect ranks or double-counting. | composition recommendation: if you need state-level aggregates (for example, count of top-3 cities per state), aggregate cities_by_state_ranked after filtering (e.g., WHERE city_rank_within_state <= N) grouped by state_name to avoid double-counting. | composition recommendation: if joining to a one-to-many table, pre-aggregate that table to one row per city_name (and state_name if needed) before joining to preserve the one-row-per-city semantics of this view.

views.name: city_rows_with_valid_state_and_population
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  city.city_name AS city_name,
  city.state_name AS state_name,
  city.population AS population
FROM city
WHERE city.state_name IS NOT NULL
  AND city.population IS NOT NULL

params.description: Rows of cities that have a non-null state and a recorded population; answers questions about city-level population and state membership.
params.when_to_use: Report population for a specific city (by city_name). | List cities within states where population is known. | Compose city-level population totals or averages for sets of cities (must re-aggregate when joining many-to-one relationships). | Filter or join other datasets to only cities that have valid state_name and population.
params.output_schema: city_name: the city name (derived from table city.column city_name). | state_name: the state name the city belongs to (derived from table city.column state_name). | population: the city's population value (derived from table city.column population).
params.metric: population = raw attribute (no aggregate) taken directly from city.population | Note: this view is at the grain of city_name (one row per city_name as selected). Any aggregation (SUM, AVG, COUNT, etc.) over population must be performed when composing at higher grain.
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_core on city.state_name = state_core.state_name — safe because state_core is one-row-per-state (one-to-one from this view's perspective on state_name) so joining will not duplicate the city-level rows or their population values. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to city_core on city_name = city_core.city_name — safe because city_core is the normalized canonical city rowset (one-row-per-city_name) so measures remain unduplicated. | UNSAFE without re-aggregation: do NOT join directly to cities_by_state_ranked (or any other one-to-many view/table keyed by state_name that emits multiple rows per city or per state ranking) without careful aggregation, because such joins can duplicate city-level population rows and will multiply the population measure. If you need summaries by state using cities_by_state_ranked, first aggregate population at the city or state level (e.g., SUM(population) GROUP BY state_name) before joining to a ranking view. | UNSAFE without re-aggregation: do NOT join to any table/view that contains multiple rows per city_name (for example: city_events, city_neighborhoods) on city_name unless you aggregate population first (e.g., keep population at city grain or use MAX/MIN as appropriate) to prevent measure inflation. | General guidance: this view's measures are raw city-level attributes. When composing up to a different grain (state, region, ranking buckets), explicitly apply aggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT) and GROUP BY the target grain before joining to or mixing with other multi-row-per-key datasets.

views.name: avg_city_population_per_state
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.state_name AS state_name,
  AVG(c.population) AS avg_city_population,
  COUNT(1) AS city_count
FROM city_core c
WHERE c.state_name IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.state_name

params.description: Average city population and city count per U.S. state (one row per state_name).
params.when_to_use: Get the average population of cities within each state and how many cities contributed to that average. | Compose higher-level state metrics that need average city size (for example, combine with state-level demographics or budgets) while preserving per-state aggregation. | Rank or filter states by average city population or by number of cities. | Serve as an aggregated building block when you need city-level summary statistics keyed by state_name without re-scanning the city table.
params.output_schema: state_name: The state name used as the grouping key. Derived from base column city_core.state_name. | avg_city_population: The average of the population values of cities in that state. Derived from AVG(city_core.population). | city_count: The number of city rows included in the aggregation for that state (COUNT(1)). Derived from COUNT(1) over rows of city_core where state_name IS NOT NULL.
params.metric: avg_city_population = AVG(city_core.population)  -- average population per city within the grouped state_name (NULL state_name rows excluded by the view's WHERE clause) | city_count = COUNT(1)  -- count of city_core rows contributing to the state's average (equivalent to COUNT(*) after WHERE state_name IS NOT NULL)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_core on state_core.state_name = avg_city_population_per_state.state_name — safe because avg_city_population_per_state has exactly one row per state_name, so joining on that key will not duplicate the aggregated measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to cities_by_state_ranked on cities_by_state_ranked.state_name = avg_city_population_per_state.state_name if cities_by_state_ranked is one-row-per-state (e.g., contains a single top-ranked city per state). This is safe only when the sibling view is guaranteed to be at most one row per state_name; otherwise re-aggregate after joining. | do NOT join directly to city_core (or any other one-to-many table keyed by state_name, e.g., a full city-level table) without re-aggregating, because city_core contains many rows per state_name and a direct join would multiply avg_city_population_per_state.city_count and distort avg_city_population unless you re-aggregate (for example, join on state_name into city_core and then GROUP BY avg_city_population_per_state.state_name, computing appropriate aggregates or using weighted expressions). | do NOT join to city_rows_with_valid_state_and_population or any selection that is multi-row-per-state without re-aggregation for the same reason: those joins would duplicate the one-row-per-state measures unless the other side is reduced to one row per state_name first. | If you need to combine this view with other multi-row datasets (for example, to compute state-level totals that sum city populations), prefer: (a) join by state_name and then re-aggregate in the outer query using SUM or AVG over the appropriate base columns; or (b) pre-aggregate the many-side to one row per state_name before joining to preserve measure semantics. | When composing metrics that involve avg_city_population together with counts or sums from other tables, be explicit about which metrics are per-state averages versus totals and avoid naive SUM(avg_city_population) across states unless that is the intended operation (i.e., treat avg_city_population as a derived per-state metric, not an additive measure).

views.description: Average city population and city count per U.S. state (one row per state_name).

In that case compute the counts from the mountains table grouped by state_name and then join to state_basic. | Do not use when you need a different join key than state_name: the view exposes only state_name as the state key, so joining on other columns may be incorrect if state_name is not the unique identifier in your query context.

views.name: cities_by_state_unnested
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.city_name AS city_name,
  c.population AS "city.population",
  c.state_name AS "city.state_name",
  s.country_name AS "state.country_name",
  s.capital AS "state.capital"
FROM city_core c
JOIN state_core s ON c.state_name = s.state_name
WHERE c.population IS NOT NULL

params.description: Provides one row per city (with non-null population) enriched with that city's state-level attributes (country and capital).
params.when_to_use: Get city-level facts (name, population) together with the state they belong to (state name, state country, state capital). | Filter or aggregate by city population while also displaying the state's country or capital. | Serve as a building block when composing further city-level analyses that need state attributes (join-safe guidance provided).
params.output_schema: city_name: The name of the city. Derived directly from base table column city_core.city_name. | city.population: The population of the city (non-null as enforced by the view WHERE clause). Derived from base table column city_core.population. | city.state_name: The state name associated with the city. Derived from base table column city_core.state_name. | state.country_name: The country name for the state that the city belongs to. Derived from base table column state_core.country_name (via join on state_name). | state.capital: The capital of the state that the city belongs to. Derived from base table column state_core.capital (via join on state_name).
params.grounded_columns: city_core.city_name | city_core.population | city_core.state_name | state_core.state_name | state_core.country_name | state_core.capital
params.metric: city.population = city_core.population  -- not an aggregate; this view filters out NULLs so the value is the raw population per city
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state-level dimension/view (e.g., state_core or state_basic) on state_name — safe because this view is one-row-per-city and the join to a one-row-per-state relation will not duplicate city rows. | Do NOT join this view directly to any one-to-many detail table keyed by city (for example, a hypothetical table of city_events or city_neighborhoods) without re-aggregating the detail first, because such joins will multiply city rows and thereby duplicate the city.population measure. | If you need to combine city-level measures with additional city-detail rows, either aggregate the detail to one row per city (e.g., SUM, COUNT grouped by city_name) before joining, or perform the join and then re-aggregate so that measures like city.population are not double-counted. | You can safely JOIN this view to other one-row-per-city views/tables keyed by city_name (for example city_base) because the key is city_name and this view's grain is city_name. | You can safely aggregate this view (e.g., AVG(city.population) per state) or join to state-level aggregates (e.g., avg_city_population_per_state) if you ensure joins are on state_name and you avoid joining both the raw city rows and the state-level aggregate simultaneously without proper grouping to prevent double-counting.

views.name: global_avg_lake_area

FROM lake
WHERE area IS NOT NULL

params.description: The global average lake area (single scalar): the mean of non-null lake.area across the lake table.
params.when_to_use: Ask for the overall average lake size across the entire dataset (a single scalar). | Compose into higher-level queries that need the global average as a constant (e.g., compare a state's or city's average lake area to the global average). | Report generation where a single global metric is required (dashboards, annotations).

params.metric: global_avg_lake_area = AVG(lake.area) over all rows where lake.area IS NOT NULL

Joining it directly to any dimensional table/view on no key (i.e., a cross join) is safe only if you intend to replicate the single scalar across rows; such replication does NOT change the metric value but will duplicate the scalar per output row — this is often acceptable for display but be aware it creates multiple rows with the same scalar. | Do NOT join this AGG view to a one-to-many detail table/view expecting the AGG to be protected from duplication unless you re-aggregate after the join. Example unsafe pattern: joining global_avg_lake_area to lake (or any table with multiple rows) and then summing or averaging without first removing the one-row nature will lead to incorrect results because the single-row scalar will be multiplied across detail rows during relational joins. | Safe composition patterns: | - Use as a constant: SELECT t.*, g.global_avg_lake_area FROM some_table t CROSS JOIN global_avg_lake_area g — safe when you only want the scalar repeated per row for comparison or display. | - Use in expressions or predicates in outer queries without joining (e.g., use the view in a subquery or CTE that returns the scalar and reference it once). | - When combining with other aggregates, always aggregate after joining. For example, to compute the difference between each state's average and the global average, compute state-level averages separately, then CROSS JOIN the single-row global_avg_lake_area and compute state_avg - global_avg in the outer SELECT. This preserves correctness because you are not attempting to sum the scalar across many rows before final aggregation. | - Do NOT join to multi-row sibling views (e.g., city_core, cities_by_state_ranked, lake detail) expecting the view to remain per-entity without re-aggregation; instead bring the scalar in via CROSS JOIN or subquery and compute per-entity comparisons in SELECT expressions. | Rationale: Because this view is aggregated to a single scalar (grain: no key columns, one row), it contains no dimensional keys. Any relational join to multi-row relations will replicate that single row across matched rows. That replication does not change the scalar value itself but will multiply result rows; if downstream queries aggregate those multiplied rows without re-normalizing, measures will be incorrectly scaled. Treat this view as a scalar constant when composing.

views.name: state_population_density
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.state_name AS state_name,
  (CAST(s.population AS REAL) / s.area) AS population_density
FROM state s
WHERE s.population IS NOT NULL
  AND s.area IS NOT NULL
  AND s.area <> 0

params.description: Returns the population density (population per unit area) for each state.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve per-state population density values for reporting or visualization. | Compare or rank states by population density. | Compose into larger queries that need a per-state density metric (e.g., join to state-level attributes). | Compute state-level correlations or aggregates where a single density value per state is required.

views.name: state_with_capital_and_density

SELECT
  state_core.state_name AS state_name,
  state_core.capital AS capital,
  state_core.population AS population,
  state_core.area AS area,
  CASE
    WHEN state_core.area IS NULL OR state_core.area = 0 THEN NULL
    ELSE (CAST(state_core.population AS REAL) / state_core.area)
  END AS population_density
FROM state_core

params.description: Provides one-row-per-state core attributes including capital, population, area, and computed population density (population per area).

Derived from state_core.capital. | population: The state's population (base count/estimate). Derived from state_core.population. | area: The state's area (same units as stored in state_core.area). Derived from state_core.area. | population_density: population / area (nullable). Computed as CASE WHEN area IS NULL OR area = 0 THEN NULL ELSE CAST(population AS REAL) / area END; uses state_core.population and state_core.area.
